meta.titre: Conditionals: choosing the verb pattern after if and after Had
meta.sous_theme: The four conditional types and inversion

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L English Language past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Before the GCE results come out, many students in Bamenda talk about what they would do if they passed and what they would have done if they had worked harder. These sentences with *if* are called conditionals, and each kind has its own verb pattern. In Paper 1 the grammar section regularly asks you to finish an *if* sentence with the right verb form. If you know the four patterns and the formal version with *Had*, these questions become easy marks.

items: The past simple of regular verbs ends in -ed; many common verbs are irregular (*go, went, gone*).
The past perfect is *had* + past participle (*had left*).
*Will* and *would* are followed by the base form of the verb (*will go, would go*).

sections.titre: The four types of conditional sentence
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Parts of a conditional

A conditional sentence has an **if-clause** (the condition) and a **main clause** (the result). The verb forms of the two clauses must match. When the if-clause comes first, a comma follows it.

| Type | Use | If-clause | Main clause | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zero | general truths and facts | present simple | present simple | If you heat ice, it melts. |
| First | a real or likely future | present simple | *will* + base verb | If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home. |
| Second | an unreal or unlikely present or future | past simple | *would* + base verb | If I had a car, I would drive you to Limbe. |
| Third | an unreal past (it did not happen) | past perfect | *would have* + past participle | If she had studied, she would have passed. |

### Key points

- Never put *will* or *would* in the if-clause. Say *If it rains*, not *If it will rain*.
- The second conditional uses a past form, but it speaks about an imagined present or future, not about the past.
- In formal English *were* is used with every person in the second conditional: *If I were you, I would wait.*
- The third conditional talks about something that did not happen, so the result did not happen either: *If we had left earlier, we would have arrived on time* means that we did not leave earlier and did not arrive on time.
- Modal verbs such as *can, may, might* and *could* can replace *will* or *would*: *If you work hard, you might win.*

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the condition is introduced by unless, provided that or as long as
variantes.contenu_markdown: *Unless* means *if ... not*. *Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus* means *If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus*. Do not add another negative after *unless*. *Provided that* and *as long as* mean *only if*: *You may go out provided that you finish your homework.*

variantes.nom: Inverted conditionals with Had and Were
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the sentence begins with Had or Were instead of If
variantes.contenu_markdown: In a formal style, *if* can be dropped and the verb put before the subject. **Had** + subject + past participle replaces *If* + subject + past perfect: *Had she studied, she would have passed.* The main clause is the same as in the third conditional. In the second conditional, **Were** + subject replaces *If* + subject + *were*: *Were I the head teacher, I would build a library.*

variantes.nom: Method for a gap at the end of the sentence
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the if-clause is given and you must choose the main clause
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name the type from the if-clause (present simple: first or zero; past simple: second; past perfect or *Had*: third). Then choose the main clause that goes with it. Reject *will* after a past form and reject *would* after a present simple.

sections.enonce_markdown:
(a) Choose the best answer. *If the bus had left earlier, we \_\_\_\_\_\_ the ceremony.* (A) would not miss (B) will not miss (C) would not have missed (D) did not miss

(b) Rewrite the sentence in (a) without the word *if*.

etapes.action: Read the verb in the if-clause.
etapes.justification: The if-clause contains *had left*, which is the past perfect.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Past perfect, so it is the third conditional.

etapes.justification: The third conditional needs *would* (or *would not*) + *have* + past participle.
(A) is a second conditional main clause, (B) is a first conditional main clause and (D) has no *would* at all.
The bus did not leave earlier, so we missed the ceremony. The sentence imagines the past in a different way, which is exactly what the third conditional does.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *If the bus had left earlier, we would not have missed the ceremony.*

etapes.justification: Put *Had* before the subject and keep the past participle; the main clause does not change.
etapes.resultat_markdown: *Had the bus left earlier, we would not have missed the ceremony.*

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The answer is **(C) would not have missed**. (b) **Had the bus left earlier, we would not have missed the ceremony.** The if-clause decides the type, and the type decides the main clause.

items.erreur_markdown: "If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: *Will* is not used in the if-clause. The present simple is used for a future condition.
items.correction_markdown: If it **rains** tomorrow, we will stay at home.

items.erreur_markdown: "If I would have time, I would visit you." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: *Would* is never used in the if-clause. The second conditional needs the past simple there.
items.correction_markdown: If I **had** time, I would visit you.

items.erreur_markdown: "If she had known the truth, she would told you." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: The third conditional main clause needs *would have* + past participle. The word *have* is missing.
items.correction_markdown: If she had known the truth, she **would have told** you.

items.erreur_markdown: "Had I knew the answer, I would have told him." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: After *Had* the past participle is needed, not the past simple. *Knew* is the past simple and *known* is the past participle.
items.correction_markdown: **Had I known** the answer, I would have told him.

items.erreur_markdown: "Unless you don't hurry, you will miss it." (a wrong sentence)
items.pourquoi_faux: *Unless* already means *if ... not*, so a second negative is wrong.
items.correction_markdown: **Unless you hurry**, you will miss it. (or: If you don't hurry, you will miss it.)

items.enonce_markdown:
Choose the correct answer.

(a) If you heat butter, it \_\_\_\_\_\_. (A) melts (B) melted (C) would melt (D) will have melted

(b) If I find your pen, I \_\_\_\_\_\_ it to you tomorrow. (A) give (B) gave (C) will give (D) had given

(c) If I were the head teacher, I \_\_\_\_\_\_ a library. (A) will build (B) would build (C) would have built (D) built

(d) If they had left earlier, they \_\_\_\_\_\_ the train. (A) would catch (B) will catch (C) would have caught (D) caught
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **A, melts**: a general truth (zero conditional).

(b) **C, will give**: a likely future (first conditional).

(c) **B, would build**: an imagined situation (second conditional).

(d) **C, would have caught**: past perfect in the if-clause, so the third conditional.

items.enonce_markdown:
Write the correct form of the verb in brackets.

(a) If we (leave) now, we will arrive before dark.

(b) If the road had been better, the journey (be) shorter.

(c) Unless you hurry, you (miss) the bus.

(d) If I (be) you, I would apologise.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **leave**: first conditional, present simple in the if-clause.

(b) **would have been**: third conditional main clause.

(c) **will miss**: *unless* means *if you do not*, and the pattern is the first conditional.

(d) **were**: second conditional, and *were* is used with all persons.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Rewrite without *if*, beginning with *Had*: If the farmer had planted early, he would have harvested more.

(b) Combine into one third conditional sentence: She did not take the medicine, so she did not recover.

(c) Rewrite with *if* instead of *unless*: Unless you work hard, you will not pass.

(d) Correct the mistake: If I would have money, I would buy a goat.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Had the farmer planted early, he would have harvested more.**

(b) **If she had taken the medicine, she would have recovered.** The two facts in the past are reversed in the third conditional.

(c) **If you do not work hard, you will not pass.** *Unless* already carries the negative idea, so *if* needs *not*.

(d) **If I had money, I would buy a goat.** *Would* is not used in the if-clause.

items_markdown: Zero: if + present simple, present simple (facts). First: if + present simple, will + base verb (likely future).
Second: if + past simple, would + base verb (unreal present or future). Third: if + past perfect, would have + past participle (unreal past).
Never use will or would in the if-clause.
Unless means if ... not, so do not add another negative.
Had + subject + past participle replaces if + past perfect, and the main clause stays *would have* + past participle.
In a gap question, the if-clause tells you the type and the type tells you the main clause.
